Article.ArticleTitle: RGS4 Overexpression in Lung Attenuates Airway Hyper-responsiveness in Mice.

Abstract.AbstractText: A cardinal feature of asthma is airway hyper-responsiveness (AHR) to spasmogens, many of which activate G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) on airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells. Asthma subtypes associated with allergy are characterized by eosinophilic inflammation in the lung due to the type 2 immune response to allergens and proinflammatory mediators that promote AHR. The degree to which intrinsic abnormalities of ASM contribute to this phenotype remains unknown. The Regulators of G protein signaling (RGS proteins) are a large group of intracellular proteins that inhibit GPCR signaling pathways. RGS2 and RGS5-deficient mice develop AHR spontaneously. Although RGS4 is upregulated in ASM from patients with severe asthma, the effects of increased RGS4 expression on AHR in vivo are unknown. Here we examined the impact of forced RGS4 overexpression in lung on AHR using transgenic (Tg) mice. Tg RGS4 was expressed in bronchial epithelium and airway smooth muscle (ASM) in vivo, and protein expression in lung was increased at least four-fold compared to that in WT mice. Lung slices from Tg mice contracted less in response to the m3 muscarinic receptor agonist methacholine (MCh) compared to WT although airway resistance in live, unchallenged mice was similar in both strains. Tg mice were partially protected from AHR induced by fungal allergen challenge due to weakened contraction signaling in ASM and reduced type 2 cytokine (IL-5, 13) levels in Tg mice compared to WT. These results provide support for the hypothesis that increasing RGS4 expression and/or function could be a viable therapeutic strategy for asthma.
